Paul's 33.4% sits within the optimal range of 25% to 40%, indicating a healthy balance between iron supply and transport capacity with no sign of either overload or deficiency.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, chronic disease, low dietary iron
biomarkers.high_causes: Haemochromatosis, iron overload, excessive supplementation

biomarkers.name: Serum Iron
biomarkers.description: Serum iron measures the amount of iron circulating in the blood at the time of the sample. It fluctuates throughout the day and with meals, so it is most useful when interpreted alongside ferritin and transferrin saturation. Paul's 20.3 is comfortably within range and confirms adequate iron availability.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, chronic disease, poor absorption, heavy bleeding
biomarkers.high_causes: Haemochromatosis, excessive supplementation, liver disease

biomarkers.name: Transferrin
biomarkers.description: Transferrin is the protein that transports iron through the bloodstream to where it is needed, primarily the bone marrow for red blood cell production. Paul's level of 2.42 is within the optimal range, confirming healthy iron transport function.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron overload, liver disease, inflammation, malnutrition
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency, pregnancy, oestrogen therapy

biomarkers.name: Total Iron Binding Capacity
biomarkers.description: Total iron binding capacity (TIBC) measures how much iron the blood could carry if all transferrin molecules were fully loaded. It is essentially a reflection of transferrin levels. Paul's TIBC of 56 is within the optimal range, consistent with the healthy transferrin and saturation levels.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron overload, liver disease, chronic inflammation
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency, pregnancy

biomarkers.name: Ferritin
biomarkers.description: Ferritin is the body's iron storage protein. It reflects how much iron is held in reserve, primarily in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Paul's ferritin of 139 is within the optimal range of 50 to 200 for a male. It is worth noting that ferritin is also an acute phase reactant, meaning it can rise with inflammation. Given the CRP of 8.9, some of this 139 may reflect the inflammatory signal rather than pure iron stores, but the level is healthy regardless.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, chronic blood loss, poor dietary intake
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron overload, haemochromatosis, inflammation, liver disease

biomarkers.name: Haemoglobin
biomarkers.description: Haemoglobin is the protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to every tissue in the body. Paul's level of 172 is marginally above the upper limit of 170 for a male. The most likely explanation is chronic carbon monoxide exposure from tobacco smoking. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen, reducing oxygen delivery, and the bone marrow compensates by increasing haemoglobin concentration. This is consistent with the marginally elevated MCH and MCHC.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, chronic disease, blood loss
biomarkers.high_causes: Smoking, dehydration, polycythaemia, chronic hypoxia, altitude

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Cell Count
biomarkers.description: The red blood cell count measures the total number of red cells per litre of blood. Paul's 5.12 is within the optimal range, indicating healthy red cell production by the bone marrow.
biomarkers.low_causes: Anaemia, bone marrow suppression, chronic disease, nutritional deficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, smoking, polycythaemia, chronic hypoxia

biomarkers.name: Haematocrit
biomarkers.description: Haematocrit measures the proportion of blood volume occupied by red blood cells. Paul's 0.492 is within the laboratory range but above the tighter optimal ceiling of 0.48, consistent with the marginally elevated haemoglobin. As with haemoglobin, this is most likely driven by compensatory erythropoiesis from smoking.
biomarkers.low_causes: Anaemia, overhydration, blood loss
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, smoking, polycythaemia, chronic hypoxia

biomarkers.name: Red Cell Distribution Width
biomarkers.description: RDW measures the variation in size among red blood cells. A higher RDW means red cells are more varied in size, which can indicate nutritional deficiencies or bone marrow stress. Paul's 12.5% is within the optimal range, confirming consistent, healthy red cell production.
biomarkers.low_causes: Generally not clinically significant when low
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, mixed anaemia, liver disease

biomarkers.name: Mean Corpuscular Volume
biomarkers.description: MCV measures the average volume of each red blood cell. Paul's 96 fL is within the optimal range, indicating normally sized red cells with no sign of the small cells seen in iron deficiency or the large cells seen in B12 or folate deficiency.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, thalassaemia, chronic disease
biomarkers.high_causes: B12/folate deficiency, alcohol excess, liver disease, hypothyroidism

biomarkers.name: Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin
biomarkers.description: MCH measures the average amount of haemoglobin packed into each red blood cell. Paul's 33.6 pg is above the upper limit of 32. This indicates that each red cell is carrying more haemoglobin than typical, which at this margin is most commonly seen with smoking. The bone marrow compensates for the reduced oxygen-carrying efficiency caused by carbon monoxide by loading more haemoglobin into each cell.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, thalassaemia
biomarkers.high_causes: B12/folate deficiency, smoking, macrocytosis

biomarkers.name: Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin Concentration
biomarkers.description: MCHC measures the concentration of haemoglobin within each red blood cell relative to its size. Paul's 350 is marginally above the upper limit of 345. As with MCH, this marginal elevation is consistent with the compensatory response to chronic carbon monoxide exposure from smoking. It is not dangerous at this level.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron deficiency, thalassaemia
biomarkers.high_causes: Spherocytosis, smoking, dehydration, laboratory artefact

biomarkers.name: Platelets
biomarkers.description: Platelets are the small cell fragments responsible for blood clotting. Paul's platelet count of 199 is within the optimal range, indicating healthy bone marrow production and no sign of clotting risk or suppression.
biomarkers.low_causes: Bone marrow suppression, viral infection, liver disease, medications
biomarkers.high_causes: Inflammation, iron deficiency, infection, bone marrow disorders

biomarkers.name: Mean Platelet Volume
biomarkers.description: MPV measures the average size of platelets. Larger platelets tend to be younger and more active. Paul's MPV of 7.3 is within the optimal range, indicating a normal, steady rate of platelet production.
biomarkers.low_causes: Bone marrow suppression, chronic inflammation
biomarkers.high_causes: Increased platelet destruction, immune thrombocytopenia, inflammation

biomarkers.name: White Blood Cell Count
biomarkers.description: The white blood cell count measures the total number of immune cells circulating in the blood. Paul's 6.14 is within the optimal range, indicating a healthy, active immune system without signs of infection or suppression.
biomarkers.low_causes: Viral infection, bone marrow suppression, autoimmune disease, medications
biomarkers.high_causes: Bacterial infection, inflammation, stress, smoking, leukaemia

biomarkers.name: Neutrophils
biomarkers.description: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cell type and the body's first responders to bacterial infection. Paul's 4.06 is within the optimal range, indicating a healthy innate immune response.
biomarkers.low_causes: Viral infection, medications, bone marrow suppression, nutritional deficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Bacterial infection, smoking, inflammation, stress, steroids

biomarkers.name: Lymphocytes
biomarkers.description: Lymphocytes are the white blood cells responsible for adaptive immunity, including the production of antibodies and the recognition of previously encountered infections. Paul's 1.51 is within the optimal range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Viral infection, HIV, steroid use, autoimmune disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Viral infection, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, autoimmune disease

biomarkers.name: Monocytes
biomarkers.description: Monocytes are white blood cells that migrate into tissues to become macrophages, engulfing pathogens and debris. Paul's 0.46 is within the optimal range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Bone marrow suppression, steroid use
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic infection, inflammation, autoimmune disease

biomarkers.name: Eosinophils
biomarkers.description: Eosinophils are white blood cells involved in allergic responses and parasitic defence. Paul's 0.08 is within the optimal range. Interestingly, despite his significantly elevated IgE of 368, eosinophils are low, which may suggest that the IgE elevation is driven by sensitisation rather than an active eosinophilic response.
biomarkers.low_causes: Steroid use, acute stress, Cushing's syndrome
biomarkers.high_causes: Allergies, asthma, parasitic infection, drug reactions

biomarkers.name: Basophils
biomarkers.description: Basophils are the rarest white blood cell type and play a role in allergic and inflammatory responses. Paul's 0.03 is within the optimal range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Steroid use, acute infection, hyperthyroidism
biomarkers.high_causes: Allergies, chronic inflammation, myeloproliferative disorders

biomarkers.name: Reticulocyte Count
biomarkers.description: Reticulocytes are young red blood cells freshly released from the bone marrow. Their percentage reflects how actively the bone marrow is producing new red cells. Paul's 1.31% is within the optimal range, confirming healthy, steady red cell production.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron/B12/folate deficiency, bone marrow suppression, chronic disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Haemolytic anaemia, blood loss, recovery from anaemia

biomarkers.name: Reticulocyte Absolute Count
biomarkers.description: The absolute reticulocyte count gives the total number of young red blood cells per litre, providing a more precise measure of bone marrow output than the percentage alone. Paul's 67.1 is within the optimal range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Iron/B12/folate deficiency, bone marrow suppression, chronic disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Haemolytic anaemia, blood loss, recovery from anaemia

biomarkers.name: Mentzer Index
biomarkers.description: The Mentzer Index (MCV divided by RBC count) helps distinguish iron deficiency anaemia from thalassaemia trait when MCV is low. Paul's MCV is normal, so this index of 18.8 is reported for context and is not applicable at present. A value above 13 favours iron deficiency over thalassaemia, and Paul's normal MCV and iron studies make this distinction unnecessary.
biomarkers.low_causes: Thalassaemia trait
biomarkers.high_causes: Iron deficiency

biomarkers.name: Reticulocyte Production Index
biomarkers.description: Reticulocyte Production Index is reported for context only and is not applicable at present, so it is not flagged.
biomarkers.low_causes: Marrow not responding to anaemia: iron, B12 or folate deficiency, marrow suppression
biomarkers.high_causes: Blood loss or haemolysis with an appropriate marrow response

biomarkers.name: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate
biomarkers.description: ESR is a non-specific marker of inflammation that measures how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube over one hour. Faster settling indicates more inflammation. Paul's ESR of 8 is within the optimal range. Interestingly, this is much less alarming than the CRP of 8.9, which suggests the CRP elevation may be relatively recent rather than long-standing, since ESR tends to rise and fall more slowly than CRP.
biomarkers.low_causes: Polycythaemia, sickle cell disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Infection, inflammation, autoimmune disease, cancer, ageing

biomarkers.name: Sodium
biomarkers.description: Sodium is the primary electrolyte controlling fluid balance and blood pressure. Paul's 141 is within the optimal range, indicating well-regulated fluid and electrolyte balance.
biomarkers.low_causes: Diuretics, excessive water intake, SIADH, adrenal insufficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, excessive salt intake, Cushing's syndrome

biomarkers.name: Potassium
biomarkers.description: Potassium is an electrolyte essential for nerve signalling, muscle contraction, and heart rhythm. Paul's level of 3.4 is marginally below the lower limit of 3.5. This may reflect sample processing delay (potassium leaks out of cells over time if the sample sits too long) or could be a genuine finding related to his ARB medication or kidney function. Given the kidney findings in this report, the GP should repeat this on a fresh sample.
biomarkers.low_causes: Diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, ARBs (rarely), renal tubular acidosis
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney disease, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, haemolysis, acidosis

biomarkers.name: Chloride
biomarkers.description: Chloride works alongside sodium and bicarbonate to maintain fluid balance and acid-base equilibrium. Paul's 96 is within the laboratory range but marginally below the tighter optimal band of 98 to 106. The low chloride is consistent with the elevated bicarbonate, as these two electrolytes tend to move in opposite directions. This pattern is characteristic of metabolic alkalosis.
biomarkers.low_causes: Vomiting, metabolic alkalosis, diuretics, SIADH
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, metabolic acidosis, kidney disease

biomarkers.name: Bicarbonate
biomarkers.description: Bicarbonate is the main buffer in the blood that maintains pH within a very narrow range. Paul's level of 33.6 is above the upper limit of 31. The most likely explanations are compensatory retention of bicarbonate by the kidneys in response to chronic respiratory acidosis from smoking (where the lungs retain carbon dioxide, and the kidneys compensate by holding onto bicarbonate to balance the pH), and/or a mild effect from the losartan. The GP should review this alongside the kidney and electrolyte findings.
biomarkers.low_causes: Metabolic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis, kidney disease, diarrhoea
biomarkers.high_causes: Metabolic alkalosis, vomiting, diuretics, compensated respiratory acidosis, ARBs

biomarkers.name: Urea
biomarkers.description: Urea is a waste product from protein metabolism, filtered by the kidneys. Paul's 5.6 is within the optimal range, suggesting adequate protein metabolism and renal clearance of this particular waste product.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low protein diet, liver disease, overhydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, kidney disease, high protein diet, GI bleeding

biomarkers.name: Creatinine
biomarkers.description: Creatinine is a waste product from muscle metabolism, filtered by the kidneys at a fairly constant rate. It is the traditional marker for estimating kidney function. Paul's creatinine of 100 is within the laboratory range but above the tighter optimal ceiling of 95 and approaching the upper limit. In a man with no resistance training, this level combined with the elevated cystatin C strengthens the case for genuine reduced kidney filtration rather than a muscle mass artefact.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low muscle mass, liver disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney disease, dehydration, high muscle mass, high protein diet

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Creatinine)
biomarkers.description: The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) from creatinine estimates how much blood the kidneys filter per minute. Above 90 is considered fully healthy, 60 to 89 is mildly reduced (Stage 2 CKD), and below 60 is moderately reduced (Stage 3). Paul's creatinine-based eGFR is 74, which sits in the mildly reduced range. This alone warrants monitoring, and the cystatin C-based eGFR of 66 gives further weight to this finding.
biomarkers.low_causes: Kidney disease, dehydration, hypertension, diabetes, medications
biomarkers.high_causes: Low muscle mass (can falsely elevate creatinine-based eGFR)

biomarkers.name: Cystatin C
biomarkers.description: Cystatin C is a small protein produced at a constant rate by all nucleated cells, freely filtered by the kidneys, and not influenced by muscle mass, diet, or sex. This makes it a more reliable marker of kidney function than creatinine, particularly in someone carrying significant extra weight with no resistance training. Paul's cystatin C of 1.33 is above the upper limit of 1.1, indicating reduced kidney filtration. The cystatin C-derived eGFR of 66 falls into Stage 2 chronic kidney disease. This is the finding that should be discussed with the GP most promptly.
biomarkers.low_causes: Generally not clinically significant when low
biomarkers.high_causes: Reduced kidney function, inflammation, thyroid disease, corticosteroid use

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Cystatin C)
biomarkers.description: This eGFR is calculated from cystatin C rather than creatinine, making it more accurate in people with very high or very low muscle mass. Paul's cystatin C-based eGFR of 66 confirms that kidney filtration is mildly reduced, consistent with the creatinine-based eGFR of 74. The lower cystatin C value likely gives the truer picture given Paul's BMI and absence of resistance training.
biomarkers.low_causes: Kidney disease, hypertension, diabetes, inflammation
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperthyroidism (can falsely lower cystatin C)

biomarkers.name: Uric Acid
biomarkers.description: Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism, cleared by the kidneys. Elevated levels are associated with gout, kidney stones, and cardiovascular risk. Paul's 394 is within the laboratory range but above the tighter optimal ceiling of 380 for a male. The mild elevation connects to the developing insulin resistance (insulin impairs uric acid excretion) and the elevated triglycerides. Weight loss and reduced fructose intake are the most effective interventions.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low purine diet, medications (allopurinol), liver disease
biomarkers.high_causes: High purine diet, alcohol, obesity, insulin resistance, kidney impairment, gout

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Creatinine + Cystatin C)
biomarkers.description: This is the combined eGFR calculated from both creatinine and cystatin C, which is considered the most accurate single estimate of kidney function. Paul's combined eGFR of 66 confirms mildly reduced kidney filtration, consistent with Stage 2 CKD. At 52 without diabetes, the most likely drivers are longstanding hypertension and the sustained inflammatory load reflected by the CRP of 8.9. A repeat in three months is essential to determine whether this is stable.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic kidney disease, dehydration, kidney strain

biomarkers.name: Urea:Creatinine Ratio
biomarkers.description: The urea to creatinine ratio helps distinguish between different causes of abnormal kidney function. A normal ratio in the context of reduced eGFR suggests intrinsic kidney disease rather than pre-renal causes like dehydration. Paul's ratio of 56 is within the optimal range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low protein intake, liver disease, overhydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, high protein intake, upper GI bleeding

biomarkers.name: hs-CRP
biomarkers.description: High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) measures low-grade systemic inflammation. It is produced by the liver in response to inflammatory signals from anywhere in the body. Levels below 1.0 are considered ideal for cardiovascular risk, 1.0 to 3.0 represents moderate risk, and above 3.0 represents higher risk. Paul's level of 8.9 is nearly nine times the ideal threshold and well above the laboratory upper limit of 5.0. The most probable sustained sources are visceral fat (which releases inflammatory cytokines continuously) and tobacco smoking. An acute illness at the time of sampling cannot be excluded, so a repeat in three months is important to confirm. This level of chronic inflammation accelerates insulin resistance, arterial damage, and kidney decline.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low inflammation, statin use, weight loss, anti-inflammatory diet
biomarkers.high_causes: Obesity, smoking, infection, chronic inflammation, autoimmune disease, cardiovascular disease

biomarkers.name: Total Protein
biomarkers.description: Total protein measures the combined albumin and globulin in the blood. Paul's 77 is within the optimal range, reflecting healthy liver synthetic function and adequate nutritional status.
biomarkers.low_causes: Malnutrition, liver disease, kidney disease, malabsorption
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, chronic infection, inflammation, myeloma

biomarkers.name: Albumin
biomarkers.description: Albumin is the most abundant protein in the blood, produced by the liver. It transports hormones, vitamins, and medications, and maintains fluid balance by keeping water inside blood vessels. Paul's albumin of 45 is within the optimal range, confirming strong liver synthetic function.
biomarkers.low_causes: Liver disease, kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome), malnutrition, inflammation
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration

biomarkers.name: Globulin
biomarkers.description: Globulins are a group of proteins including immunoglobulins (antibodies) and transport proteins. Paul's 32 is within the optimal range, consistent with his healthy individual immunoglobulin levels.
biomarkers.low_causes: Immunodeficiency, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic infection, inflammation, autoimmune disease, liver disease

biomarkers.name: Alkaline Phosphatase
biomarkers.description: ALP is an enzyme found in the liver, bones, and bile ducts. Elevated levels can indicate bile duct obstruction, bone disease, or liver damage. Paul's 83 is within the optimal range, confirming no sign of bile duct or bone pathology.
biomarkers.low_causes: Malnutrition, hypothyroidism, zinc deficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Bile duct obstruction, bone disease, liver disease, Paget's disease

biomarkers.name: Total Bilirubin
biomarkers.description: Bilirubin is the yellow pigment produced when red blood cells are broken down, processed by the liver, and excreted in bile. Paul's 18 is within the laboratory range but above the tighter optimal ceiling of 15. With all liver enzymes clean, this likely reflects either normal individual variation or a mild degree of Gilbert's syndrome, a common, harmless inherited trait affecting bilirubin processing that is present in around 5 to 10% of the population. It is not a concern.
biomarkers.low_causes: Generally not clinically significant
biomarkers.high_causes: Gilbert's syndrome, liver disease, haemolytic anaemia, bile duct obstruction

biomarkers.name: ALT
biomarkers.description: ALT (alanine aminotransferase) is the liver enzyme most specific to liver cell damage. It is the single best screening marker for liver inflammation. Paul's ALT of 29 is within the tighter optimal threshold of below 30 for a male. At a BMI of 48.5, a clean ALT is a genuinely reassuring finding because the liver is under significant metabolic load from excess weight, yet it shows no sign of damage.
biomarkers.low_causes: Generally not clinically significant
biomarkers.high_causes: Fatty liver disease, hepatitis, medications, alcohol, obesity

biomarkers.name: AST
biomarkers.description: AST (aspartate aminotransferase) is found in the liver, heart, and muscle. Unlike ALT, it is not specific to the liver. Paul's AST of 31 is within the optimal range, consistent with the clean ALT and GGT.
biomarkers.low_causes: B6 deficiency, uraemia
biomarkers.high_causes: Liver disease, muscle damage, heart disease, medications

biomarkers.name: Gamma GT
biomarkers.description: Gamma GT (GGT) is a liver enzyme that rises with alcohol use, bile duct problems, metabolic stress, and certain medications. It is the most sensitive liver enzyme for detecting alcohol-related strain. Paul's GGT of 26 is within the laboratory range of 4 to 73 for a male but marginally above the tighter optimal ceiling of 25. This is a very minor finding and at BMI 48.5, the fact that GGT is barely above the strictest optimal limit is a genuine positive, indicating the liver is handling the metabolic load well.
biomarkers.low_causes: Generally not clinically significant
biomarkers.high_causes: Alcohol, fatty liver, bile duct obstruction, medications, metabolic syndrome

biomarkers.name: Amylase
biomarkers.description: Amylase is an enzyme produced by the pancreas and salivary glands that breaks down starch. Paul's 58 is within the optimal range, confirming healthy pancreatic function.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis
biomarkers.high_causes: Acute pancreatitis, salivary gland disease, bowel obstruction

biomarkers.name: Lipase
biomarkers.description: Lipase is a pancreatic enzyme that breaks down fats. It is more specific to the pancreas than amylase. Paul's 48 is within the optimal range, ruling out pancreatic inflammation.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic pancreatitis (late stage), cystic fibrosis
biomarkers.high_causes: Acute pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, kidney disease

biomarkers.name: Calcium
biomarkers.description: Calcium is essential for bone health, muscle contraction, nerve signalling, and blood clotting. Paul's total calcium of 2.44 is within the optimal range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Vitamin D deficiency, hypoparathyroidism, kidney disease, malabsorption
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperparathyroidism, cancer, excessive vitamin D, dehydration

biomarkers.name: Corrected Calcium
biomarkers.description: Corrected calcium adjusts the total calcium for the albumin level, giving a more accurate picture of the physiologically active calcium. Paul's corrected calcium of 2.37 is within the optimal range, confirming healthy calcium balance.
biomarkers.low_causes: Vitamin D deficiency, hypoparathyroidism, kidney disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperparathyroidism, cancer, excessive vitamin D

biomarkers.name: Phosphate
biomarkers.description: Phosphate works with calcium for bone health and is involved in energy production (as part of ATP). Paul's 0.8 is within the laboratory range but marginally below the tighter optimal band of 0.9 to 1.4. At this level, with calcium and PTH both within range, this is a very minor finding and may reflect dietary intake or timing of the sample.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor dietary intake, vitamin D deficiency, hyperparathyroidism, refeeding syndrome
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney disease, hypoparathyroidism, excessive supplementation

biomarkers.name: Magnesium
biomarkers.description: Magnesium is involved in over 300 enzymatic reactions including energy production, muscle and nerve function, blood sugar control, and blood pressure regulation. Paul's 0.90 is within the optimal range of 0.85 to 1.05. This is reassuring given the hypertension and developing insulin resistance, as magnesium deficiency worsens both.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor dietary intake, alcohol, diuretics, diabetes, malabsorption
biomarkers.high_causes: Kidney disease, excessive supplementation, adrenal insufficiency

biomarkers.name: Vitamin D
biomarkers.description: Vitamin D is essential for calcium absorption, bone health, immune function, and mood regulation. Paul's level of 95 sits within the optimal range of 75 to 120. At a BMI of 48.5, this is a genuinely impressive result because fat tissue sequesters vitamin D, making it significantly harder to maintain adequate levels. Paul is clearly either supplementing effectively or getting regular sun exposure.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low sunlight exposure, dark skin, obesity, malabsorption, ageing
biomarkers.high_causes: Excessive supplementation, granulomatous disease

biomarkers.name: Parathyroid Hormone
biomarkers.description: PTH is the hormone that regulates calcium and phosphate levels. When calcium drops, PTH rises to pull calcium from bones and increase absorption from the gut. Paul's PTH of 2.683 is within the optimal range, confirming healthy calcium regulation and no sign of parathyroid pathology.
biomarkers.low_causes: Hypoparathyroidism, excess vitamin D, high calcium
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, kidney disease, low calcium

biomarkers.name: Vitamin B12
biomarkers.description: Vitamin B12 is essential for nerve function, red blood cell production, and DNA synthesis. It plays a critical role in energy metabolism and cognitive function. Paul's B12 of 325 is within the laboratory range but below the optimal threshold of 500. At this level, the body has enough to prevent clinical deficiency, but research suggests that levels above 500 are associated with better neurological function and energy. Given that Paul reports fatigue and brain fog, optimising B12 with sublingual methylcobalamin supplementation may help.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor dietary intake (especially vegetarian/vegan), malabsorption, pernicious anaemia, metformin, ageing
biomarkers.high_causes: Supplementation, liver disease, myeloproliferative disorders

biomarkers.name: Serum Folate
biomarkers.description: Folate (vitamin B9) is essential for DNA synthesis, red blood cell production, and neural function. Paul's folate of 11 is within the optimal range, confirming adequate dietary intake.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor dietary intake, alcohol, malabsorption, medications (methotrexate)
biomarkers.high_causes: Supplementation, high dietary intake

biomarkers.name: Total Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Total cholesterol is the sum of all cholesterol fractions: LDL, HDL, and VLDL. Paul's 4.6 is within the desirable range of below 5.18. Total cholesterol alone is a crude measure because it does not distinguish between protective HDL and harmful LDL. The more informative markers are ApoB, the LDL:HDL ratio, and the triglyceride:HDL ratio, discussed in their individual entries.
biomarkers.low_causes: Malnutrition, hyperthyroidism, liver disease, statins
biomarkers.high_causes: High saturated fat diet, familial hypercholesterolaemia, hypothyroidism, obesity, diabetes

biomarkers.name: Triglycerides
biomarkers.description: Triglycerides are the fats circulating in the blood, primarily derived from dietary carbohydrates and fats. Paul's 2.78 is well above the desirable fasting threshold of 1.70 and nearly three times the optimal target of below 1.0. Elevated triglycerides are one of the hallmarks of metabolic syndrome and are driven by excess carbohydrate intake, insulin resistance, obesity, and physical inactivity. They are the central finding in Paul's lipid profile because they suppress HDL production, increase VLDL, promote the formation of small dense LDL particles, and independently increase cardiovascular risk. Reducing refined carbohydrates, losing weight, and increasing aerobic exercise are the most effective interventions.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low-fat diet, malnutrition, hyperthyroidism
biomarkers.high_causes: High carbohydrate diet, obesity, insulin resistance, alcohol, diabetes, hypothyroidism

biomarkers.name: VLDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) is the particle that carries triglycerides from the liver to the tissues. Paul's 1.26 is above the upper limit of 0.78, directly reflecting the elevated triglycerides. As triglycerides come down through dietary changes and weight loss, VLDL will fall with them.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low-fat diet, familial hypobetalipoproteinaemia
biomarkers.high_causes: Obesity, insulin resistance, high carbohydrate diet, alcohol, diabetes

biomarkers.name: HDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: HDL (high-density lipoprotein) is the protective cholesterol that removes excess cholesterol from artery walls and transports it back to the liver for processing. Higher is better. Paul's HDL of 1.1 sits above the high-risk threshold of 1.04 but below the desirable level of 1.55 and well below the optimal target of 1.4 for a male. Low HDL is one of the defining features of metabolic syndrome and is directly suppressed by high triglycerides. The most effective ways to raise HDL are regular aerobic exercise, weight loss, and reducing refined carbohydrate intake. Adding resistance training also helps.
biomarkers.low_causes: Obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, high-carbohydrate diet, insulin resistance
biomarkers.high_causes: Regular exercise, moderate alcohol consumption, genetic factors

biomarkers.name: LDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) is the cholesterol particle most associated with arterial plaque formation. Paul's LDL of 2.43 is within the laboratory range of 0.5 to 3.0 and below the tighter optimal ceiling of 2.6. While the absolute LDL number looks reasonable, the Atherogenic Index of Plasma suggests that a higher proportion of these particles are the small, dense type that penetrates artery walls more easily. This is driven by the elevated triglycerides rather than by LDL concentration itself.
biomarkers.low_causes: Statins, low-fat diet, hyperthyroidism, malnutrition
biomarkers.high_causes: High saturated fat diet, obesity, familial hypercholesterolaemia, hypothyroidism

biomarkers.name: TC:HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: The total cholesterol to HDL ratio is a quick measure of cardiovascular risk. Paul's ratio of 4.18 is within the laboratory limit of below 4.5 but above the tighter optimal ceiling of 3.5. The ratio is elevated because HDL is low (1.1) rather than because total cholesterol is high (4.6). Improving HDL through exercise and weight loss will bring this ratio into the optimal zone.
biomarkers.low_causes: High HDL, low total cholesterol
biomarkers.high_causes: Low HDL, high total cholesterol, metabolic syndrome

biomarkers.name: Non-HDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL and captures all atherogenic (artery-damaging) particles: LDL, VLDL, and remnant cholesterol. Paul's 3.5 is within the laboratory limit of below 4.0 but above the tighter optimal ceiling of 3.0. The excess is driven primarily by the elevated VLDL from high triglycerides.
biomarkers.low_causes: Statins, low-fat diet, hyperthyroidism
biomarkers.high_causes: Elevated LDL, elevated VLDL/triglycerides, metabolic syndrome

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein A1
biomarkers.description: ApoA1 is the main structural protein of HDL particles and a measure of the functional capacity of the protective cholesterol system. Paul's 1.42 is above both the minimum threshold of 1.20 and the optimal target of 1.40, which is a positive finding and suggests that the HDL particles present, while fewer than ideal, are functioning well.
biomarkers.low_causes: Metabolic syndrome, smoking, physical inactivity, genetic factors
biomarkers.high_causes: Regular exercise, moderate alcohol consumption, oestrogen, genetic factors

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein B
biomarkers.description: ApoB is the single best predictor of cardiovascular risk because it counts the total number of atherogenic (artery-damaging) lipoprotein particles in the blood. Each LDL, VLDL, and remnant particle carries exactly one ApoB molecule. Paul's ApoB of 0.85 is within the desirable threshold of below 0.9 but above the tighter optimal target of 0.8. At this level, the particle count is only marginally elevated and is being driven primarily by the high VLDL from elevated triglycerides rather than by LDL concentration. Reducing triglycerides through dietary change and weight loss should bring ApoB below 0.8.
biomarkers.low_causes: Statins, low-fat diet, hyperthyroidism, malnutrition
biomarkers.high_causes: Metabolic syndrome, high saturated fat diet, familial hypercholesterolaemia, insulin resistance

biomarkers.name: ApoB/A1 Ratio
biomarkers.description: The ApoB to ApoA1 ratio is the single best summary metric for the balance between harmful and protective lipoproteins. Below 0.7 is lower risk, and Paul's 0.60 falls within the optimal zone. This is a genuine positive and reflects the fact that while triglycerides are elevated and HDL is low, the absolute particle counts are not yet dramatically imbalanced. Maintaining and improving this ratio through lifestyle change is the goal.
biomarkers.low_causes: High HDL, low LDL, exercise, healthy diet
biomarkers.high_causes: Metabolic syndrome, high LDL, low HDL, insulin resistance

biomarkers.name: Lipoprotein(a)
biomarkers.description: Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), is a genetically determined lipoprotein particle that is structurally similar to LDL but carries an additional protein called apolipoprotein(a). It deposits cholesterol in artery walls, promotes clot formation, and drives local inflammation. Unlike LDL, Lp(a) is entirely inherited and cannot be changed by diet, exercise, or most medications. Paul's Lp(a) is below 25, within the normal range of below 32. This is genuinely useful information because it means that all of the cardiovascular risk in his lipid profile is driven by modifiable lifestyle factors rather than by an inherited, fixed particle. It also means that dietary changes, weight loss, and exercise have the full potential to normalise his lipid picture.
biomarkers.low_causes: Genetic factors (favourable)
biomarkers.high_causes: Genetic factors (unfavourable, inherited, not modifiable)

biomarkers.name: Creatine Kinase
biomarkers.description: Creatine kinase (CK) is an enzyme released from damaged muscle cells. Elevated levels indicate muscle injury from intense exercise, trauma, or in rare cases, a muscle-wasting condition. Paul's CK of 124 is within the optimal range, confirming no significant muscle damage.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low muscle mass, sedentary lifestyle
biomarkers.high_causes: Intense exercise, muscle injury, rhabdomyolysis, statin use, hypothyroidism

biomarkers.name: Free T4
biomarkers.description: Free T4 (thyroxine) is the main circulating thyroid hormone, produced by the thyroid gland in response to TSH. Paul's FT4 of 19.8 sits near the top of the optimal range of 14 to 20, indicating excellent thyroid hormone output.
biomarkers.low_causes: Hypothyroidism, pituitary disease, iodine deficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperthyroidism, thyroiditis, excessive thyroid medication

biomarkers.name: TSH
biomarkers.description: TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone) is produced by the pituitary gland to regulate thyroid function. When thyroid hormones are low, TSH rises to stimulate more production; when they are adequate, TSH stays low. Paul's TSH of 1.8 sits in the optimal zone of 1.0 to 2.5, confirming that the thyroid is producing exactly the right amount of hormone without being pushed.
biomarkers.low_causes: Hyperthyroidism, excessive thyroid medication, pituitary disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Hypothyroidism, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, iodine deficiency, recovery from illness

biomarkers.name: Free T3
biomarkers.description: Free T3 (triiodothyronine) is the active thyroid hormone that cells actually use. Most T3 is converted from T4 in the liver, kidneys, and tissues. Paul's FT3 of 5.0 is within the optimal range of 4.5 to 6.5, confirming adequate conversion and active thyroid hormone availability.
biomarkers.low_causes: Hypothyroidism, low T4, poor conversion, illness, calorie restriction
biomarkers.high_causes: Hyperthyroidism, T3 thyrotoxicosis

biomarkers.name: Thyroid Peroxidase Antibodies
biomarkers.description: TPO antibodies target an enzyme in the thyroid gland and, when elevated, indicate autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis). Paul's level is below 6.6 (reported as less than 6.6), well within the normal range of below 13.8, ruling out autoimmune thyroid attack.
biomarkers.low_causes: No autoimmune thyroid disease (normal finding)
biomarkers.high_causes: Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, other autoimmune conditions

biomarkers.name: Thyroglobulin Antibodies
biomarkers.description: Thyroglobulin antibodies target the protein from which thyroid hormones are made. When elevated above 4.4, they suggest autoimmune thyroid disease. Paul's level is below 1.3 (reported as less than 1.3), consistent with more than 80% of the population who have undetectable levels. This confirms no autoimmune thyroid disease.
biomarkers.low_causes: No autoimmune thyroid disease (normal finding)
biomarkers.high_causes: Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, thyroid cancer monitoring

biomarkers.name: FT3:FT4 Ratio
biomarkers.description: The FT3 to FT4 ratio estimates how efficiently the body converts the storage form of thyroid hormone (T4) into the active form (T3). Paul's ratio of 0.253 is within the laboratory range but marginally below the optimal band of 0.27 to 0.40. This suggests that conversion could be slightly more efficient, though the absolute FT3 level of 5.0 is comfortably within the optimal range, so the clinical significance is minimal. Selenium, zinc, and adequate calorie intake support optimal conversion.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor T4 to T3 conversion, low ferritin or selenium, chronic illness
biomarkers.high_causes: Overactive thyroid, stimulant use

biomarkers.name: PSA
biomarkers.description: PSA (prostate-specific antigen) is a protein produced by the prostate gland. It is used as a screening marker for prostate health, with elevated levels potentially indicating benign enlargement, infection, or in some cases, prostate cancer. Paul's PSA of 0.64 is very low and well within the ideal range at 52, indicating excellent prostate health.
biomarkers.low_causes: Healthy prostate, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride)
biomarkers.high_causes: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, prostate cancer, recent ejaculation, cycling

biomarkers.name: Free PSA
biomarkers.description: Free PSA measures the fraction of PSA that is not bound to proteins. The ratio of free to total PSA helps distinguish benign prostate conditions from cancer. A higher free PSA ratio is reassuring. Paul's free PSA of 0.35 is within range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Generally not clinically significant in isolation
biomarkers.high_causes: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis

biomarkers.name: PSA Ratio
biomarkers.description: The PSA ratio (free PSA divided by total PSA) helps refine prostate cancer risk. A ratio above 0.19 (19%) is normal, and higher ratios are more reassuring. Paul's ratio of 0.547 (54.7%) is strongly reassuring and, combined with the very low total PSA, indicates excellent prostate health.
biomarkers.low_causes: Higher cancer risk (lower free proportion)
biomarkers.high_causes: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (reassuring finding)

biomarkers.name: CA 19-9
biomarkers.description: CA 19-9 is a tumour marker associated with pancreatic and gastrointestinal cancers. It is not a diagnostic test but is used for screening and monitoring. Paul's 5.31 is well within the normal range of below 37, providing reassurance.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding
biomarkers.high_causes: Pancreatic cancer, biliary obstruction, liver disease, pancreatitis

biomarkers.name: CEA
biomarkers.description: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) is a tumour marker associated with colorectal and other cancers. The reference range is higher for smokers (0 to 4.1) than non-smokers (0 to 2.3). Paul's CEA of 1.82 is within the smoker range and also within the non-smoker range, providing reassurance. Smoking cessation would be expected to reduce this further.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding
biomarkers.high_causes: Colorectal cancer, lung cancer, breast cancer, liver disease, smoking, inflammatory bowel disease

biomarkers.name: IgG
biomarkers.description: IgG is the most abundant immunoglobulin and the main antibody providing long-term immunity against bacteria and viruses. Paul's IgG of 12.8 is within the laboratory range, indicating a healthy adaptive immune response.
biomarkers.low_causes: Immunodeficiency, medications (immunosuppressants), nephrotic syndrome
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, liver disease, myeloma

biomarkers.name: IgM
biomarkers.description: IgM is the first antibody produced in response to a new infection. It is a marker of acute immune response. Paul's IgM of 1.3 is within the laboratory range, indicating no sign of acute infection.
biomarkers.low_causes: Immunodeficiency, medications
biomarkers.high_causes: Acute infection, Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia, autoimmune disease

biomarkers.name: IgA
biomarkers.description: IgA is the antibody that protects mucosal surfaces including the gut lining, respiratory tract, and urinary tract. It is also the antibody class used in coeliac disease screening. Paul's IgA of 2.4 is within the laboratory range, confirming healthy mucosal immunity and also validating the coeliac screen (which uses IgA-based antibodies).
biomarkers.low_causes: Selective IgA deficiency (common), immunodeficiency
biomarkers.high_causes: Liver disease, coeliac disease, chronic infection, autoimmune disease

biomarkers.name: IgE
biomarkers.description: IgE is the antibody class most associated with allergic reactions and parasitic defence. Paul's IgE of 368 is more than three and a half times the upper limit of 100, indicating significant allergic sensitisation. Common causes include environmental allergens (house dust mite, animal dander, pollen, mould) and certain food sensitivities. Smoking can also contribute to elevated IgE. Parasitic infection is a less common cause in the UK. This level warrants a conversation with the GP about specific allergen testing (a RAST panel or skin prick testing) to identify the trigger, particularly as unrecognised allergy can contribute to fatigue, nasal congestion, and immune system burden.
biomarkers.low_causes: Immunodeficiency (rare), immunosuppressive therapy
biomarkers.high_causes: Allergic conditions (eczema, asthma, hay fever), parasitic infection, smoking, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis

biomarkers.name: Rheumatoid Factor
biomarkers.description: Rheumatoid factor is an antibody associated with rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune conditions. This result is pending and will be reviewed when available.
biomarkers.high_causes: Rheumatoid arthritis, other autoimmune diseases, chronic infection

biomarkers.name: Tissue Transglutaminase IgA
biomarkers.description: Tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) is the primary screening test for coeliac disease, an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten. Paul's result of 2.93 is well below the threshold of 7.19 and reported as negative, ruling out coeliac disease as a cause of his symptoms. This test is only valid on a gluten-containing diet, which Paul follows.
biomarkers.low_causes: Normal finding (no coeliac disease)
biomarkers.high_causes: Coeliac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis

biomarkers.name: Total Antioxidant Activity
biomarkers.description: Total antioxidant activity measures the overall capacity of the blood to neutralise free radicals. Paul's TAA of 2.23 is above the laboratory range of 1.3 to 1.77. This is not a concern and most likely reflects dietary antioxidant intake from fruits, vegetables, tea, or supplementation. Elevated bilirubin (his is 18) also contributes to antioxidant capacity. This is a benign finding.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor dietary antioxidant intake, oxidative stress, chronic disease
biomarkers.high_causes: High dietary antioxidant intake, supplementation, elevated bilirubin

biomarkers.name: Cortisol
biomarkers.description: Cortisol is the body's primary stress hormone, produced by the adrenal glands. It follows a daily rhythm, peaking in the early morning and declining through the day. Paul's cortisol of 302 is within the optimal range for a morning sample, indicating healthy adrenal function and an appropriate stress response.
biomarkers.low_causes: Adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), pituitary disease
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic stress, Cushing's syndrome, prednisolone use, acute illness

biomarkers.name: Oestradiol
biomarkers.description: Oestradiol is the primary oestrogen in men, produced by the aromatase enzyme converting testosterone in fat tissue and other organs. Paul's oestradiol of 105 is within the laboratory range of below 146.1 but above the tighter optimal ceiling of 100. At a BMI of 48.5, increased aromatase activity in visceral fat converts more testosterone to oestradiol, which is one mechanism suppressing his testosterone below the optimal range. Weight loss reduces aromatase activity and helps rebalance this ratio.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low body fat, aromatase inhibitors, hypogonadism
biomarkers.high_causes: Obesity (aromatase in fat tissue), liver disease, medications

biomarkers.name: Progesterone
biomarkers.description: Progesterone in men is produced in small amounts by the adrenal glands and testes. It plays a minor role compared to women. Paul's 1.62 is within the normal range and is not a clinically significant marker in males.
biomarkers.low_causes: Not clinically significant in males at this level
biomarkers.high_causes: Adrenal tumour, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (rare)

biomarkers.name: Luteinising Hormone
biomarkers.description: LH is a pituitary hormone that stimulates the testes to produce testosterone. Paul's LH of 6.6 is within the optimal range, indicating that the pituitary is signalling the testes appropriately. The fact that LH is normal while testosterone is below optimal suggests the testes are responding but the peripheral conversion of testosterone to oestradiol in fat tissue is the more likely cause of the suboptimal level.
biomarkers.low_causes: Pituitary disease, steroid use, obesity
biomarkers.high_causes: Primary hypogonadism (testicular failure), Klinefelter syndrome, ageing

biomarkers.name: Follicle Stimulating Hormone
biomarkers.description: FSH is a pituitary hormone that, in men, supports sperm production. Paul's FSH of 5.82 is within the optimal range, confirming healthy pituitary-gonadal signalling.
biomarkers.low_causes: Pituitary disease, steroid use, obesity
biomarkers.high_causes: Primary testicular failure, Klinefelter syndrome, ageing

biomarkers.name: Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Testosterone is the primary male sex hormone, responsible for energy, muscle mass, bone density, libido, mood, and cognitive function. Paul's testosterone of 14.4 is within the laboratory range of 8.4 to 28.7 but below the optimal threshold of 18. At a BMI of 48.5, the most likely mechanism is increased aromatase activity in visceral fat tissue converting testosterone to oestradiol (which is 105, above the optimal ceiling). Cannabis use may also contribute to lower testosterone. The most effective intervention is weight loss, which reduces aromatase activity, lowers oestradiol, and allows testosterone to rise. This finding is relevant to Paul's symptoms of fatigue and poor exercise recovery.
biomarkers.low_causes: Obesity, ageing, pituitary disease, medications (opioids), cannabis use, sleep deprivation, chronic illness
biomarkers.high_causes: Steroid use, tumours (adrenal or testicular), congenital adrenal hyperplasia

biomarkers.name: Prolactin
biomarkers.description: Prolactin is a pituitary hormone primarily associated with milk production in women. In men, elevated levels can suppress testosterone and cause sexual dysfunction. Paul's prolactin of 62 is within the optimal range, ruling out prolactinoma or medication-induced elevation as a cause of his suboptimal testosterone.
biomarkers.low_causes: Generally not clinically significant
biomarkers.high_causes: Prolactinoma, medications (antipsychotics, antidepressants), hypothyroidism, stress

biomarkers.name: Free Androgen Index
biomarkers.description: The Free Androgen Index (FAI) estimates the proportion of testosterone that is biologically active by comparing total testosterone to SHBG. Paul's FAI of 39.56 is within the laboratory range but below the optimal threshold of 50. This reflects the suboptimal total testosterone of 14.4 rather than excess SHBG binding, as SHBG at 36.4 is within a healthy range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low testosterone, high SHBG, obesity, ageing
biomarkers.high_causes: High testosterone, low SHBG, PCOS (females)

biomarkers.name: DHEA Sulphate
biomarkers.description: DHEA-S is a hormone produced by the adrenal glands that serves as a precursor to both testosterone and oestrogen. It declines naturally with age. Paul's DHEA-S of 2,506.8 ug/dL (converted from 6.8 umol/L) is within the optimal range for his age, indicating healthy adrenal function.
biomarkers.low_causes: Ageing, adrenal insufficiency, chronic illness, steroid use
biomarkers.high_causes: Adrenal tumour, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, PCOS (females)

biomarkers.name: Sex Hormone Binding Globulin
biomarkers.description: SHBG is a protein produced by the liver that binds testosterone and oestradiol, controlling how much of each is free and biologically active. Paul's SHBG of 36.4 is within the optimal range of 25 to 55. This is a healthy level that is not excessively binding testosterone, so the suboptimal testosterone is a production or conversion issue rather than a binding issue.
biomarkers.low_causes: Obesity, insulin resistance, hypothyroidism, anabolic steroids
biomarkers.high_causes: Ageing, liver disease, hyperthyroidism, oestrogen

biomarkers.name: Free Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Free testosterone is the fraction of total testosterone not bound to SHBG or albumin, and therefore available for the body to use directly. Paul's free testosterone of 0.271 is within the laboratory range but marginally below the optimal threshold of 0.3. This reflects the suboptimal total testosterone rather than excessive SHBG binding.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low total testosterone, high SHBG, obesity, ageing
biomarkers.high_causes: High total testosterone, low SHBG, steroid use

biomarkers.name: Bioavailable Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Bioavailable testosterone includes both free testosterone and the fraction loosely bound to albumin, representing the testosterone actually accessible to tissues. Paul's bioavailable testosterone of 6.64 is within the optimal range of 4 to 9, which is reassuring and indicates that despite the suboptimal total testosterone, the amount reaching the tissues is adequate. This is because SHBG is at a healthy level and is not excessively binding testosterone.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low total testosterone, high SHBG, obesity, poor sleep, chronic stress
biomarkers.high_causes: Testosterone therapy, anabolic steroid use

biomarkers.name: Free Oestradiol Index
biomarkers.description: The Free Oestradiol Index estimates the proportion of oestradiol that is unbound and biologically active. This is reported for context and is not applicable as a standalone diagnostic marker at present.

biomarkers.name: Urine pH
biomarkers.description: Urine pH reflects the acidity or alkalinity of the urine. A pH of 7.5 is mildly alkaline, which is within the normal physiological range and can be influenced by diet, hydration, and medication.

biomarkers.name: Urine Protein
biomarkers.description: Urine protein tests for the presence of protein in the urine, which can indicate kidney damage. Paul's result is negative, which is reassuring alongside the kidney findings and confirms no protein leak from the kidneys.

biomarkers.name: Urine Ketones
biomarkers.description: Urine ketones are produced when the body burns fat for energy instead of glucose, as occurs during fasting, very low-carbohydrate diets, or uncontrolled diabetes. Paul's result is negative, consistent with his standard mixed diet and normal glucose control.

biomarkers.name: Urine Glucose
biomarkers.description: Glucose in the urine indicates blood sugar levels high enough to overwhelm the kidneys' ability to reabsorb it. Paul's result is negative, consistent with his well-controlled fasting glucose and HbA1c.

biomarkers.name: Specific Gravity
biomarkers.description: Specific gravity measures the concentration of the urine. Paul's 1.015 is within the normal range of 1.005 to 1.030, indicating adequate hydration.

biomarkers.name: Urobilinogen
biomarkers.description: Urobilinogen is a breakdown product of bilirubin. Elevated levels in urine can indicate liver disease or haemolytic anaemia. Paul's result is negative, consistent with his healthy liver function.

biomarkers.name: Urine Casts
biomarkers.description: Urinary casts are cylindrical structures formed in the kidney tubules. Their presence can indicate kidney disease. Paul's result is negative, which is reassuring alongside the kidney findings.

biomarkers.name: Urine White Blood Cells
biomarkers.description: White blood cells in the urine can indicate a urinary tract infection or kidney inflammation. Paul's result of less than 1 is not significant, confirming no urinary tract infection.

biomarkers.name: Urine Red Blood Cells
biomarkers.description: Red blood cells in the urine can indicate kidney disease, urinary tract infection, or other urological conditions. Paul's result of less than 1 is not significant, confirming no blood in the urine.

biomarkers.name: Urine Nitrites
biomarkers.description: Nitrites in the urine suggest the presence of bacteria that convert nitrate to nitrite, indicating a urinary tract infection. Paul's result is negative, ruling out bacterial infection.

biomarkers.name: Bacterial Count
biomarkers.description: The bacterial count quantifies any bacteria present in the urine sample. This result is pending and will be reviewed when available. Given the negative nitrites and white cells, significant infection is unlikely.

biomarkers.name: Urine Culture
biomarkers.description: The urine culture identifies specific organisms growing in the urine and their antibiotic sensitivities. This result is pending. Given the negative nitrites and white cells, significant infection is unlikely.

biomarkers.name: Neutrophil:Lymphocyte Ratio
biomarkers.description: The neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is a simple marker of the balance between innate (neutrophil) and adaptive (lymphocyte) immunity. A ratio between 1 and 3 is within the laboratory range, and between 1 and 2 is considered optimal. Paul's NLR of 2.69 is within the laboratory range but above the optimal ceiling of 2.0. This likely reflects the low-grade systemic inflammation indicated by the CRP of 8.9 and is consistent with the overall inflammatory picture driven by visceral adiposity and smoking.
biomarkers.low_causes: Lymphocytosis, neutropenia
biomarkers.high_causes: Inflammation, infection, smoking, stress, obesity

biomarkers.name: Platelet:Lymphocyte Ratio
biomarkers.description: The platelet to lymphocyte ratio (PLR) is another inflammatory marker that combines platelet and lymphocyte counts. Paul's PLR of 131.8 is within the optimal range, indicating no significant inflammatory shift in this particular metric.
biomarkers.low_causes: Thrombocytopenia, lymphocytosis
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic inflammation, infection

biomarkers.name: Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index
biomarkers.description: The Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index (SII) combines neutrophils, platelets, and lymphocytes into a single measure of systemic inflammation. Paul's SII of 535 is within the laboratory range but above the tighter optimal ceiling of 450. This is consistent with the CRP-driven inflammatory picture and the mildly elevated NLR.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low inflammation, lymphocytosis
biomarkers.high_causes: Chronic inflammation, infection, malignancy

biomarkers.name: TG:HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: The triglyceride to HDL ratio is one of the best surrogate markers for insulin resistance and small dense LDL particles. A ratio below 0.87 is optimal, and below 1.5 is within the laboratory range. Paul's ratio of 2.53 is well above both thresholds, driven by the elevated triglycerides of 2.78 and the suppressed HDL of 1.1. This ratio confirms the metabolic syndrome pattern and the predominance of atherogenic small dense LDL particles. It will improve in tandem with triglycerides falling and HDL rising through dietary change, weight loss, and exercise.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low triglycerides, high HDL, exercise, healthy diet
biomarkers.high_causes: Insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, high carbohydrate diet, obesity, physical inactivity

biomarkers.name: Remnant Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Remnant cholesterol is the cholesterol carried by triglyceride-rich remnant particles (calculated as total cholesterol minus HDL minus LDL). These remnants are highly atherogenic because they penetrate artery walls easily. Paul's remnant cholesterol of 1.07 is above the upper limit of 0.8, reflecting the elevated triglycerides and VLDL. This is an independent cardiovascular risk factor and will improve as triglycerides normalise through dietary change and weight loss.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low triglycerides, healthy diet
biomarkers.high_causes: Elevated triglycerides, insulin resistance, obesity, high-carbohydrate diet

biomarkers.name: Lp(a)-Corrected LDL
biomarkers.description: Lp(a)-corrected LDL removes the cholesterol contribution of Lp(a) particles from the total LDL number, showing the LDL that is genuinely modifiable through lifestyle and medication. Paul's corrected LDL of 2.35 is within the laboratory range. Because his Lp(a) is low, the correction makes only a small difference, confirming that effectively all of his LDL is the conventional, lifestyle-responsive type.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low LDL, statins, low-fat diet
biomarkers.high_causes: Diet high in saturated fat, familial hypercholesterolaemia

biomarkers.name: Atherogenic Index of Plasma
biomarkers.description: The Atherogenic Index of Plasma (AIP) is calculated from the logarithm of triglycerides divided by HDL and is one of the strongest predictors of small dense LDL particle predominance. Values above 0.21 indicate higher cardiovascular risk. Paul's AIP of 0.403 is above the upper limit, confirming a predominance of the small, dense LDL particles that are most effective at penetrating artery walls. This is driven entirely by the elevated triglycerides and suppressed HDL, and will improve as those normalise through dietary change and weight loss.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low triglycerides, high HDL, exercise, healthy diet
biomarkers.high_causes: High triglycerides, low HDL, insulin resistance

biomarkers.name: LDL:HDL Ratio (Castelli II)
biomarkers.description: The LDL to HDL ratio (Castelli II index) provides another view of the balance between harmful and protective cholesterol. Paul's ratio of 2.21 is within the optimal zone of below 2.5, which is a positive finding and reflects the fact that while HDL is below ideal, LDL is relatively well controlled.
biomarkers.low_causes: High HDL, low LDL
biomarkers.high_causes: Raised LDL, low HDL

biomarkers.name: Albumin:Globulin Ratio
biomarkers.description: The albumin to globulin ratio reflects the balance between liver synthetic function (albumin) and immune or inflammatory protein production (globulin). Paul's A/G ratio of 1.41 is within the optimal range, confirming healthy liver function and no evidence of chronic immune activation or liver disease.
biomarkers.low_causes: Liver disease, chronic infection, autoimmune disease, nephrotic syndrome
biomarkers.high_causes: Immunodeficiency (rare when both components are in range)

biomarkers.name: FIB-4 Index
biomarkers.description: FIB-4 is a calculated score that estimates the likelihood of liver fibrosis (scarring) using age, ALT, AST, and platelet count. Paul's score of 1.5 is marginally above the 1.45 threshold. However, the score is being inflated by two factors: at 52, the age term adds weight, and his relatively low ALT of 29 makes the denominator smaller, paradoxically pushing the score up. With every direct liver marker (ALT, AST, GGT, bilirubin, albumin) within range, and the APRI at 0.389 (well within the ideal zone), this score does not indicate liver fibrosis. It is worth mentioning to the GP for context but does not warrant concern.
biomarkers.low_causes: Healthy liver, young age
biomarkers.high_causes: Liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, age

biomarkers.name: APRI
biomarkers.description: The APRI (AST to Platelet Ratio Index) estimates the likelihood of significant liver fibrosis. Paul's APRI of 0.389 is well within the optimal range of below 0.5 and far below the threshold of 1.5 for significant fibrosis. This confirms no evidence of liver scarring, consistent with the clean ALT, AST, and GGT.
biomarkers.low_causes: Healthy liver
biomarkers.high_causes: Liver fibrosis, cirrhosis

biomarkers.name: NAFLD Fibrosis Score
biomarkers.description: The NAFLD Fibrosis Score uses age, BMI, diabetes status, ALT, AST, platelets, and albumin to estimate the likelihood of advanced fibrosis in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Paul's score of 0.311 is within the indeterminate zone (between -1.455 and 0.676). The score is being pushed up by the BMI of 48.5 and age of 52 rather than by any liver enzyme abnormality. All direct liver markers are clean, and the APRI of 0.389 argues against significant fibrosis. The score is driven by the calculation inputs rather than by liver disease.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low BMI, young age, healthy liver
biomarkers.high_causes: Advanced fibrosis in fatty liver disease

biomarkers.name: AST:ALT Ratio (De Ritis)
biomarkers.description: The De Ritis ratio (AST divided by ALT) helps distinguish between different causes of liver enzyme elevation. A ratio above 2 suggests alcoholic liver disease, while a ratio below 1 is more common in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Paul's ratio of 1.07 is within the optimal range and, with both enzymes at healthy levels, simply confirms a balanced liver enzyme profile.
biomarkers.low_causes: Fatty liver, viral hepatitis
biomarkers.high_causes: Alcohol-related liver disease, cirrhosis, muscle injury

biomarkers.name: Anion Gap
biomarkers.description: The anion gap is calculated from sodium, potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate to assess acid-base balance. Paul's anion gap of 14.8 is within the optimal range, indicating no significant metabolic acidosis.
biomarkers.low_causes: Hypoalbuminaemia, bromide ingestion, laboratory error
biomarkers.high_causes: Metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, toxic ingestion), kidney failure

biomarkers.name: Glucose-Corrected Sodium
biomarkers.description: Glucose-Corrected Sodium is reported for context only and is not applicable at present, so it is not flagged.

biomarkers.name: Albumin-Corrected Anion Gap
biomarkers.description: The albumin-corrected anion gap adjusts the standard anion gap for albumin levels, since low albumin can mask an elevated gap. Paul's corrected anion gap of 14.8 is reported for context and is consistent with normal acid-base balance.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low albumin, laboratory error
biomarkers.high_causes: Dietary acid load, reduced kidney clearance, ketosis, dehydration
